title: The lower a group of organisms, the more widely it tends to range

fields.label: Label
fields.value: The lower a group of organisms, the more widely it tends to range

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Organisms lower in the scale of nature tend to range more widely than higher ones, because they change more slowly and their seeds and eggs are minute and suited to distant transport.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: namely, that the lower any group of organisms is, the more widely it is apt to range.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter XII, “Geographical Distribution, continued”; section “On colonisation from the nearest source with subsequent modification”. Scope: plants and animals across taxonomic groups considered 'lower' and 'higher'

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch12-17: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.61

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Range size is measurable, but the explanatory variable requires a substantial and contestable modern reinterpretation. Existing data can test trait-specific proxies, not Darwin's ordering as stated.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Replace the obsolete lower-to-higher scale with prespecified traits such as body size, propagule size, structural complexity or clade age, and model geographic range size across species. The claim is supported only for operationalizations showing a robust negative association with range.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Occurrence density and taxonomy differ sharply among groups.

The 'scale of nature' has no accepted measurable ordering.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.72
data adequacy: 0.7
operationalizability: 0.35
data existence: 0.82
discriminating power: 0.45

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The sentence has a measurable biogeographic pattern only after 'lower' is replaced by a grade, body size or propagule size, and those mappings disagree. Checklist and occurrence databases can support a proxy test inside plants or vertebrates and cannot support one across all of life. Sampling bias is large enough that many outcomes would still be compatible with both the claim and its opposite.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Using an explicit proxy for 'lower', such as non-seed plants versus seed plants or small-bodied versus large-bodied animals, compare geographic range size or number of regions occupied. The claim is confirmed if the lower proxy has systematically larger ranges after correcting for the number of records, and refuted if range size is unrelated to that proxy or runs the other way.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
'Lower in the scale of nature' has several competing modern proxies, and they do not rank the same organisms together.

Better-studied large organisms can look either more or less widespread depending on whether range is measured as a map or as a list of records.

Recorded ranges of microbes and minute invertebrates are dominated by where people have sampled, not by where the organisms live.
